summary:
Lunar Analyzer is a mission-planning decision support system developed for Lunar South Pole landing site selection and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication analysis.
Because the Moon has a 1.5° axial tilt and no atmosphere, the Sun hovers within a ±1.5° band along the horizon, where crater ridges can block solar power and DTE links for days. Unlike static 3D tools such as Moon Trek, Lunar Analyzer adds time dynamics and automated risk classification. Our engine integrates multi-resolution NASA LOLA terrain maps (5 m-240 m DEM + ERR) with 2026-2035 NAIF SPICE orbital kernels, scanning 3,600 azimuths up to 200 km to compute finite solar disk visibility (fsun) and geometric DTE line-of-sight. It simulates +24/+48/+72 h launch delays, factors in elevation error margins (ERR) to assign transparent GREEN, YELLOW, RED, or GRAY statuses and ranks candidates via an objective Pareto front, Dual Explorer and Engineer interfaces serve both students and mission planners with identical calculations. Validated against NASA JPL Horizons (4.14 × 10⁻⁷°, max error, 12/12 tests passed), Lunar Analyzer enables reliable, scalable site pre-screening for Artemis and future Mars polar missions.
details:
Lunar Analyzer is a web-based decision support system that evaluates candidate landing sites in the Lunar South Pole (-80° to -90° planetocentric latitude) for continuous solar power and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication. Existing platforms such as Moon Trek and QuickMap display static 3D terrain, whereas Lunar Analyzer adds a time dimension, launch delay simulation, and uncertainty-aware classification. When a user selects a coordinate, landing time in UTC, mission duration, and buffer window, the backend merges multi-resolution NASA LOLA Digital Elevation Models (240 m, 80 m, and 5 m) with elevation error rasters (ERR) and 2026–2035 NAIF SPICE orbital kernels in the MOON_ME_DE440_ME421 reference frame. It scans 3,600 azimuths out to a 200 km radius to extract a 360° local horizon profile, then calculates finite solar disk visibility (f_sun, accounting for the Sun's 0.53° angular diameter) and geometric DTE line-of-sight across every time step.

Our team designed the model around the physical realities of the lunar poles. Because the Moon has only a 1.5° axial tilt and no atmosphere, the Sun travels within a ±1.5° band near the horizon, meaning a 100-meter crater ridge can block sunlight or Earth visibility for days. Instead of inventing arbitrary weighted scores, we evaluate nominal terrain alongside conservative elevation error bounds (ERR ±k) and launch slip scenarios (+0 h, +24 h, +48 h, and +72 h) to assign each site one of four transparent statuses: GREEN, YELLOW, RED, or GRAY. When comparing multiple candidates, we apply an objective Pareto front so mission planners can examine trade-offs between solar availability and DTE windows without hidden scoring bias. To make the tool accessible to both students and mission engineers without simplifying the physics, we paired one shared calculation engine with two interfaces: an Explorer Mode featuring a 4-step wizard with pre-indexed 5 m LOLA tiles (such as Connecting Ridge, Shackleton Rim, and Malapert Massif), and an Engineer Mode that exposes coordinate frames, solar panel and antenna heights, constraint violation intervals, and raw data exports.

We developed the calculation engine and automated verification suite in Python, combining NAIF SPICE ephemeris kernels, multi-resolution raster terrain processing, and a REST API connected to an interactive web frontend. To verify scientific accuracy, we compared our Sun and Earth sky angles against NASA JPL Horizons, achieving a maximum angular difference of 4.14 × 10⁻⁷° (well within our 0.005° threshold), and checked terrain slopes against official NASA PGDA slope maps with a 0.08° median difference across a 12-test validation suite.

By turning static elevation maps into repeatable, auditable pre-screening analyses—while explicitly reporting model boundaries rather than acting as a landing certificate—Lunar Analyzer helps mission teams identify robust landing windows and delay risks. Built on 2026–2035 SPICE data, it supports Artemis-era planning over the coming decade. Because its horizon and ephemeris architecture is modular, battery depletion and RF link budgets can be added directly, allowing the same framework to adapt to Mars polar missions as well as Earth applications such as solar power plant shadow forecasting and telecommunications line-of-sight planning in mountainous terrain.
